issue: After United States v. Cotton, does a defect in an indictment that fails to allege any federal crime deprive the court of jurisdiction, or are all indictment defects non-jurisdictional?

sides.position: Cotton's rule that indictment defects are non-jurisdictional does not extend to an indictment that fails to allege any federal crime at all, so such a defect remains jurisdictional.
cases: United States v. McIntosh, 704 F.3d 894, 901–03 (11th Cir. 2013)

sides.position: Cotton applies broadly. Defects in an indictment, including failure to state an offense, are not jurisdictional.
cases: United States v. De Vaughn, 694 F.3d 1141, 1148–49 (10th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Cothran, 302 F.3d 279, 283 (5th Cir. 2002)
United States v. Muresanu, No. 18-3690 (7th Cir. 2020)

this_court: Adopts the Fifth and Tenth Circuits' broad reading: defects in an indictment are not jurisdictional, rejecting the Eleventh Circuit's narrower view.
quote: The circuits are split on the proper interpretation of Cotton.
cite: United States v. Ionel Muresanu, No. 18-3690 (7th Cir. 2020)
